Female Tidepool gunnels ultimately reach a total length of 30 cm [Li = 30 cm], a size that distinguishes them from the smaller males in this intertidal species. This maximum size, recorded from field surveys of Pholis nebulosa, represents the asymptotic body length achieved by the largest individuals in the population. By comparison with the closely related Pholis gunnellus, where the length at sexual maturation occurs at roughly half the ultimate length, the total length at puberty for female Tidepool gunnels is estimated at 15 cm [Lp = 15 cm]. This transition marks the onset of gonadal activity and the beginning of reproductive competence in this iteroparous blenny. The allometric relationship between length and mass, derived from measurements across a wide size range of conspecifics, indicates that a female achieving her ultimate length will have a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 174 grams [Wwi = 174 grams]. This substantial adult body mass, which is among the larger values recorded for pholidid fishes in the North Pacific, reflects the species’ capacity for storing energy reserves necessary for surviving the variable conditions of tidepool habitats and for provisioning multiple clutches over successive breeding seasons.

Newly hatched larvae emerge from demersal eggs at a remarkably small size, with the wet weight at birth estimated at 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams]. This neonatal body mass is derived from the average egg diameter of 2 millimeters observed in the congeneric species Pholis gunnellus, a value that aligns well with direct observations of egg size in Pholis nebulosa. The yolk-sac larva, which is entirely lecithotrophic during its first days after eclosion, relies on this endogenous yolk reserve to sustain its early development before the onset of exogenous feeding. Given the small initial mass, the larvae are particularly vulnerable to starvation during the critical period of yolk-sac resorption, a phase during which mouth opening and retinal differentiation must occur before the Point of No Return is reached. The rapid depletion of these limited lipid stores means that successful transition to planktivory is essential within a narrow temporal window, and field studies suggest that mortality during this early larval stage can exceed ninety percent under poor prey conditions.

The maximum reproductive rate of Tidepool gunnel has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 18.3 °C [T = 18.3 °C]. At this thermal regime, females produce on average 20 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 20 eggs per clutch], and they deposit approximately one clutch each day [F_R_i = approximately one clutch each day] during the peak of the spawning season, yielding a daily reproductive output of about 20 eggs per day [Ri = about 20 eggs per day]. This remarkably high daily fecundity is facilitated by the species’ batch-spawning strategy, in which vitellogenesis proceeds continuously to sustain the near-daily deposition of adhesive eggs into nest sites guarded by the male. The measured spawning rate is among the highest recorded for intertidal fish of comparable body size, though it is partially offset by the energetic costs of nest defense and egg fanning. The strong temperature dependence of this process is evident when compared to trials conducted at cooler temperatures, where inter-clutch intervals lengthen considerably and total seasonal output declines.

Gravid females approaching their asymptotic size are capable of sustaining high fecundity over several months, reflecting a life-history strategy optimized for the predictable but brief windows of productivity characteristic of temperate intertidal ecosystems. Brooding males, which attend the egg masses until hatching, incur substantial metabolic costs during the incubation period, and their body condition often declines measurably over successive clutches. The pelagic larval phase that follows hatching lasts several weeks, during which the planktonic larvae disperse widely before undergoing metamorphosis and settling into intertidal habitats as benthic juveniles. This pelagic-benthic transition represents a critical demographic bottleneck, and year-class strength is heavily influenced by oceanographic conditions that govern larval transport and food availability during the preflexion and postflexion stages. Post-settlement juveniles grow rapidly as they exploit the abundant microcrustacean prey in rock pools, achieving the 15 cm [Lp = 15 cm] length at puberty within their first full year of benthic life. Field recapture data indicate that sexual maturation consistently occurs at this size threshold, and no females smaller than this benchmark have ever been observed with hydrated oocytes or other signs of imminent spawning. Such a defined size at maturation is typical of many intertidal pholidids, ensuring that reproductive effort is deferred until a body size sufficient to support the energetic demands of nest-guarding and repeated spawnings is attained.

The lifespan of Tidepool gunnel has been documented from mark-recapture studies and captive observations, which indicate that individuals survive for 5 years [am = 5 years] when reared at 18.3 °C [T = 18.3 °C]. This longevity, which is equivalent to approximately 1825 days, exceeds that reported for several smaller-bodied intertidal blennies but is shorter than the extended lifespans observed in deeper-living pholidids. The temperature dependence of physiological aging processes is evident from comparisons with populations inhabiting cooler waters, where individuals may persist for additional years at the cost of reduced annual reproductive output. Senescent adults in the final year of life show declining body condition, reduced fecundity, and slower fin regeneration following injury. Natural mortality in the wild primarily results from predation by larger fish and avian predators, combined with the physiological stress of desiccation during extreme low tides. Despite these pressures, the combination of a moderate longevity and high reproductive output has proven sufficient to sustain stable populations across the species’ range from the Sea of Japan to the western Aleutian Islands.
